# Age Calculator Lab

- How Old Am I?: https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/how-old-am-i/

> 166 free, browser-based calculators for age, dates, birthdays, pregnancy, work milestones and calendar planning, plus 146 guides explaining the methods behind them. No account, no server-side processing of calculator inputs, and every page states its method and limits.

Written and reviewed by Navjeet Kamboj. Results are informational: clinical, legal, financial, school, employment and benefits decisions are governed by the relevant manual, policy or authority.

## Guides
- [Age in Korean: How to Say Your Age & Ask "How Old Are You?"](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/age-in-korean/): Learn how to say age in Korean, ask "How old are you?", use 살 and 나이, and give your age naturally with common Korean phrases and examples.
- [Did Korea Change Its Age System? Understanding the 2023 Korean Age Change](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/korean-age-system-change/): Did Korea get rid of Korean age? Learn what changed on June 28, 2023, how South Korea standardized full-age counting, and where separate age rules remain.
- [How Old Am I in Korean Age? Calculate Your Korean Age](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/how-old-am-i-in-korean-age/): Wondering how old you are in Korean age? Enter your birth date to compare your traditional Korean age with your international age and see the difference.
- [How to Calculate Korean Age: Formula, Examples & Calculator](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/how-to-calculate-korean-age/): Step-by-step arithmetic guide to traditional Korean age: Current Year − Birth Year + 1. Includes birthday comparisons and worked examples.
- [Korean Age vs International Age: What's the Difference?](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/korean-age-vs-international-age/): Learn why Korean age can be 1 or 2 years higher than international and American age, with birthday comparisons and timelines.
- [SSC CGL Age Limit 2026: Post-Wise Age Limit, DOB & Age Relaxation](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/ssc-cgl-age-limit/): Comprehensive guide to SSC CGL 2026 age limits. Explore post-wise age bands (18–27, 20–30, 18–30, 18–32), the 1 August 2026 crucial date, category relaxations & eligible DOB ranges.
- [SSC CGL Post-Wise Age Limit 2026: Age Limit for Every Post](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/ssc-cgl-post-wise-age-limit/): Check official SSC CGL post-wise age limits for 2026 across all ministries and departments. Searchable table for 18–27, 20–30, 18–30, and 18–32 posts.
- [SSC CGL DOB Eligibility 2026: Check Your Eligible Date of Birth](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/ssc-cgl-dob-eligibility/): Check SSC CGL DOB eligibility for 2026. Learn the age-reckoning date, post-wise DOB ranges, cutoff rules, age relaxation and how to verify your eligibility.
- [SSC CGL Age Relaxation 2026: OBC, SC, ST, PwBD & Ex-Servicemen](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/ssc-cgl-age-relaxation/): Check SSC CGL age relaxation 2026 for OBC, SC, ST, PwBD, ex-servicemen and eligible government employees, with rules, deduction formulas and examples.
- [SSC CGL Eligibility Criteria 2026: Age, Qualification, Nationality & More](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/ssc-cgl-eligibility-criteria/): Complete guide to SSC CGL eligibility criteria 2026. Check age limits, educational qualifications, final-year student rules, nationality, and required documents.
- [What Is Years of Service? Meaning, Tenure & Length of Employment](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/what-is-years-of-service/): What does years of service mean? Understand employee tenure, length of employment, calendar duration vs qualifying service, work anniversaries, and milestones.
- [How to Calculate Years of Service: Years, Months & Days](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/how-to-calculate-years-of-service/): Learn how to calculate years of service accurately in years, months, and days. Complete methodology, worked example, leap-year handling, and qualifying service rules.
- [Years of Service vs Years of Experience: What's the Difference?](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/years-of-service-vs-years-of-experience/): Understand the key difference between years of service and years of experience. Learn why single-employer tenure differs from total career experience, how overlapping jobs work, and how to calculate both.
- [How Many Days Have I Worked? Calculate Total Days of Service](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/how-many-days-have-i-worked/): Calculate exactly how many days you have worked. Learn the +1 inclusive counting rule, business weekdays vs calendar days, leap year February 29 effects, and HR service auditing.
- [How to Calculate Employee Tenure From a Start Date](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/how-to-calculate-employee-tenure/): Learn how to calculate employee tenure from a hire or start date. Step-by-step calendar calculation, current vs former employees, breaks, and worked examples.
- [How to Calculate Your Work Anniversary: Date, Next Anniversary & Countdown](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/how-to-calculate-work-anniversary/): Learn how to calculate your work anniversary date, find your next upcoming anniversary, count down remaining days, and track major career milestones accurately.
- [How to Calculate Exact Age in Years, Months and Days](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/calculate-exact-age-years-months-days/): Exact age is a calendar interval built from three separate counts, which is why dividing days by 365 never reproduces it.
- [Chronological Age: What It Measures and What It Doesn't](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/chronological-age-explained/): Chronological age is elapsed calendar time between two dates — objective, reproducible, and different from every other kind of age.
- [Calendar Age vs Decimal Age: Which One Does Your Form Want?](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/calendar-age-vs-decimal-age/): Calendar age preserves years, months and days; decimal age expresses the same span as a fraction of an average year.
- [Working Out Your Age on a Past Date](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/calculate-age-on-past-date/): A historical age calculation uses the event date as the reference point, not today — and that is the input people forget to change.
- [How Old Will I Be on a Future Date?](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/calculate-age-on-future-date/): Future-age planning compares a birth date with a specific target date — and near a birthday, the year alone is not enough.
- [Leap-Day Birthdays: Ageing Normally, Celebrating Awkwardly](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/leap-day-birthdays-age-calculation/): People born on 29 February age continuously like everyone else — it is the anniversary convention in non-leap years that varies.
- [Why Month Length Changes the Answer](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/why-month-length-changes-age-results/): Months run from 28 to 31 days, so any calculation that treats them as a fixed size drifts away from the calendar immediately.
- [Age Difference vs Date Difference: Same Arithmetic, Different Question](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/age-difference-vs-date-difference/): Age difference compares two birth dates; date difference compares any two dates. The calculation is identical and the interpretation is not.
- [Finding a Birth Year From a Known Age](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/find-birth-year-from-age/): An age and a date usually identify a range of possible birth dates, not one — because the birthday may or may not have passed.
- [How Many Days Old Am I?](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/how-many-days-old-am-i/): Total days lived is a count of midnights crossed, which makes it exact — no month lengths, no conventions, no rounding.
- [Age in Weeks, Months and Hours: Picking the Right Unit](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/age-in-weeks-months-hours-guide/): Each unit answers a different question, and some of them are exact while others are derived approximations.
- [Why Every Age You Record Needs Its Date](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/record-reference-date-with-age/): Age is elapsed time, so a recorded age is only true on one day — and nothing in the number signals when that day was.
- [Chronological Age for Standardised Assessments](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/chronological-age-standardized-assessments/): Norm-referenced tests select an age band from the child's age on the test date, which makes the reference date as important as the arithmetic.
- [The Y;M;D Format for Age Records](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/ymd-semicolon-format-guide/): Y;M;D writes completed years, months and days as three separate fields — it is a presentation format for a calendar result, not a decimal number.
- [Choosing the Correct Assessment Date](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/choose-assessment-date-age-calculation/): The reference date is a decision made by the test manual, not a convenience — and it is the input most often left on a default.
- [BRIGANCE Age Calculation: What the Calculator Does and Doesn't Do](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/brigance-age-calculation-basics/): BRIGANCE screening workflows need chronological age on the screening date, in the format the product materials specify.
- [Pearson-Style Chronological Age Calculation](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/pearson-style-age-calculation/): Several widely used instruments record calendar age in years, months and days for norm-table selection — the format is shared, the rules are not.
- [The Age Calculation Errors That Actually Occur in School Evaluations](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/age-calculation-errors-school-evaluations/): Almost every real error is an input problem or a reference-date problem — not a failure of arithmetic.
- [Age Bands and Cutoff Dates: Working Near a Boundary](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/age-bands-cutoff-dates/): A band turns a continuous age into a category, which means a one-day difference at the wrong point changes the category.
- [Documenting an Age Calculation So It Can Be Rebuilt](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/document-age-calculations/): A recorded age that cannot be reproduced is not evidence — it is a number someone once believed.
- [Corrected Age for Premature Babies: A Parent's Guide](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/corrected-age-premature-babies/): Corrected age subtracts how early a baby arrived from their chronological age, so development is compared against the right timeline.
- [Adjusted Age vs Chronological Age: Which Number Goes Where](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/adjusted-vs-chronological-age/): The two ages answer different questions, and most confusion comes from a record that shows one without saying which.
- [Gestational Age vs Fetal Age: Two Weeks Apart by Definition](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/gestational-age-vs-fetal-age/): Gestational age counts from the last menstrual period; fetal age estimates time since conception, and is about two weeks less.
- [How Due Dates Are Calculated — and What They Actually Predict](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/pregnancy-due-date-calculation/): The standard model adds 280 days to the last menstrual period, producing the centre of a range rather than a scheduled event.
- [Tracking a Baby's Age in Weeks](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/track-baby-age-in-weeks/): Weeks are the right unit in early infancy because a calendar month is too coarse for how fast things change.
- [Tracking a Baby's Age in Calendar Months](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/track-baby-age-in-months/): Calendar-month age advances on the matching day of each month, which means it does not advance every 30 days.
- [When Does Corrected Age Stop Being Used?](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/when-to-stop-corrected-age/): There is no universal cutoff — the point at which correction stops depends on the purpose, the child and the guidance being followed.
- [Corrected Age: A Worked Example, Step by Step](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/prematurity-age-calculation-example/): Doing the two calculations separately — chronological age, then the prematurity interval — is what keeps the result reproducible.
- [How a Birthday Countdown Actually Works](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/birthday-countdown-guide/): Build this year's birthday first, then advance a year only if it has already gone — that single rule handles every case including the day itself.
- [What a Golden Birthday Is, and When Yours Falls](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/golden-birthday-explained/): Your golden birthday is the one where your age matches the day of the month you were born — turning 18 on the 18th.
- [Half Birthdays: Six Months, Not 182 Days](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/half-birthday-planning/): A half birthday is six calendar months after your birthday, which is somewhere between 181 and 184 days depending on where it falls.
- [When Will You Be 10,000 Days Old?](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/ten-thousand-days-old/): Ten thousand days is about 27 years and 4 months — and unlike a birthday, the exact date requires actual counting.
- [Your Billion-Second Birthday](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/billion-seconds-birthday/): One billion seconds is 11,574 days — about 31 years and 8 months — and the exact moment depends on a birth time most people do not have.
- [Planning a Milestone Birthday Date](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/milestone-birthday-planning/): A milestone birthday is a calendar anniversary, so it is found by adding whole years to the birth date — not by adding days.
- [Working Out School Starting Age](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/school-starting-age-guide/): School entry compares a child's date of birth with an official cutoff date, and the cutoff is local, specific and subject to change.
- [Kindergarten Cutoff Dates: Reading the Rule Precisely](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/kindergarten-cutoff-date/): A cutoff is a policy boundary, and the wording around it decides outcomes for children born within a day of it.
- [Calculating Age on an Exam Date](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/age-on-exam-date/): Exam age limits are measured on a date named by the awarding body, which is often not the date you register.
- [Estimating Age at Graduation](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/graduation-age-calculation/): Graduation age is exact once the ceremony date is fixed, and a planning estimate until then.
- [Finding the Date You Reach Driving Age](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/driving-age-eligibility-date/): The birthday is one condition among several — graduated licensing systems add training, supervision and waiting periods on top.
- [The Date You Reach Voting Age — and the Deadline That Matters More](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/voting-age-date-guide/): Reaching voting age is a birthday calculation; being able to vote usually depends on a registration deadline weeks earlier.
- [Calculating Years of Service Accurately](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/years-of-service-calculation/): Calendar duration is arithmetic; credited service is policy. The two are frequently different and only one of them decides entitlements.
- [Work Anniversaries and Service Milestones](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/work-anniversary-guide/): A work anniversary repeats the start date each year; a service milestone counts completed years. They usually agree and occasionally do not.
- [Calculating a Retirement Date From a Target Age](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/retirement-date-target-age/): Reaching a target age is arithmetic. When benefits actually start is a plan rule, and the two dates are rarely the same.
- [What Is Pensionable Age? Pensionable Age vs Retirement Age Explained](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/what-is-pensionable-age/): Understand what pensionable age means, how UK State Pension age differs from retirement age and private pension access (NMPA), and when you become eligible by date of birth.
- [UK State Pension Age by Date of Birth: Complete Guide](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/uk-state-pension-age-by-date-of-birth/): Find your UK State Pension age and eligibility date by date of birth. Complete guide covering cohorts born in 1960, 1961, 1970, 1978, transition rules, and timetable updates.
- [When Can I Get My State Pension? How to Check Your State Pension Age](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/when-can-i-get-state-pension/): Find out when you can get your UK State Pension, how State Pension age is calculated, how to check your date, and where to find your official forecast.
- [State Pension Age vs Retirement Age: What's the Difference?](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/state-pension-age-vs-retirement-age/): State Pension age and retirement age are fundamentally different. Learn how UK State Pension eligibility differs from personal retirement, workplace schemes, and private pension access.
- [How Is State Pension Age Calculated? UK Rules Explained](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/how-is-state-pension-age-calculated/): Explanation of how UK State Pension age is determined from date of birth, legislation, the State Pension age timetable, and transitional rules.
- [Early Retirement Age in the UK: What Age Can You Retire?](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/early-retirement-age-uk/): Understand early retirement ages in the UK, minimum pension access rules (NMPA), retiring at 55, 60, 62, or 65, and how to calculate a target retirement date.
- [Can I Retire Before State Pension Age? Early Retirement in the UK Explained](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/can-i-retire-before-state-pension-age/): Understand how early retirement works in the UK, how to bridge the gap until State Pension age, and how private and workplace pensions interact with statutory milestones.
- [Career Length vs Employment Duration](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/career-length-calculation/): Employment duration measures one continuous role; career length spans several, and the gaps and overlaps have to be handled deliberately.
- [Planning With Business Days: Buffers That Survive December](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/business-days-date-planning/): Business-day planning fails in the same place every time — the final fortnight, where weekends and holidays cluster.
- [Dog Years to Human Years: Why Size Changes Everything](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/dog-years-human-years/): The seven-to-one rule fails at both ends — dogs mature far faster in year one, then age at rates that depend heavily on size.
- [Cat Years to Human Years](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/cat-years-human-years/): Cats mature fast and then age slowly, and unlike dogs, size and breed make comparatively little difference.
- [Estimating a Tree's Age From Its Trunk](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/estimate-tree-age/): Measure the circumference, convert to diameter, multiply by a species growth factor — and treat the result as a broad estimate.
- [Your Age on Other Planets](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/planetary-age-explained/): Divide your Earth age by another planet's orbital period and you get how many of its years you have lived through.
- [Estimating How Many Heartbeats You Have Lived](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/heartbeats-lived-estimate/): Multiply elapsed minutes by an assumed average heart rate — an arithmetic exercise whose answer is entirely governed by the rate you pick.
- [Estimating Lifetime Breaths](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/breaths-lived-estimate/): Elapsed minutes multiplied by an assumed breathing rate — a calculation dominated entirely by the rate you assume.
- [How Much of Your Life Have You Spent Asleep?](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/sleep-time-lived-estimate/): Days lived multiplied by average nightly sleep, divided by 24 — a straight-line model that ignores how much sleep changes across a life.
- [Western Zodiac Date Ranges and Why Sources Disagree](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/zodiac-sign-date-ranges/): Sun-sign dates come from a fixed tropical scheme, but cusp dates shift by a day between years and between sources.
- [Chinese Zodiac Years and the Lunar New Year Boundary](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/chinese-zodiac-year-boundaries/): The animal changes at Lunar New Year, not on 1 January — so January and early-February births frequently belong to the previous year's animal.
- [Birthstones and Birth Flowers by Month](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/birthstone-birth-flower-guide/): Both are month-based traditions with more than one authoritative list, so the answer depends on which tradition you are following.
- [Life Path Numbers: The Method and Its Variations](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/life-path-number-guide/): Reduce the digits of a birth date to a single number, keeping 11, 22 and 33 — though practitioners disagree on how to reduce.
- [Adding Months to a Date Without Breaking It](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/add-months-to-date-safely/): Adding a month means moving the month and keeping the day number — except when the destination month is too short to hold it.
- [Business Days vs Calendar Days: Reading the Definition](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/business-days-vs-calendar-days/): A business-day count depends on three separate decisions, and the phrase itself specifies none of them.
- [Gregorian Leap Year Rules, and Why the Shortcut Fails](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/gregorian-leap-year-rules/): Divisible by four, except centuries, except centuries divisible by four hundred — three rules that exist to correct an eleven-minute error.
- [Years, Months and Days Between Two Dates: A Worked Example](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/date-difference-worked-example/): Following the count step by step shows exactly where the common shortcuts go wrong.
- [Weekday, Day of Year and Week Number: Three Different Labels](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/weekday-and-day-of-year/): One date carries several positional labels, and each uses a different convention — including which year it belongs to.
- [Inclusive vs Exclusive Date Counting](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/inclusive-exclusive-date-counting/): Two tools counting the same two dates can differ by one, two, or zero — depending on which endpoints each decided to count.
- [Completed Age vs Running Age](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/completed-age-vs-running-age/): Completed age counts birthdays already reached; running age describes the year of life in progress, and is one higher.
- [Why Two Age Calculators Give Different Answers](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/why-age-calculators-disagree/): Almost every disagreement is a convention difference rather than an error — and there are only about six conventions in play.
- [February 29 Birthdays: Anniversaries, Gaps and Legal Age](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/february-29-birthday-timeline/): A leap-day birth date recurs every four years, with an eight-year gap around most century years — and the legal anniversary is decided by jurisdiction.
- [Finding the Midpoint Between Two Dates](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/date-midpoint-explained/): The midpoint is the halfway instant, which lands on a whole date only when the span contains an even number of days.
- [Inclusive Date Counting: Ten Cases Where It Changes the Answer](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/inclusive-date-counting-examples/): The convention is simple; recognising which one a real document means is the hard part. These are the cases that come up.
- [Adding Business Days Without Losing Count](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/add-business-days-correctly/): Adding business days means stepping forward one day at a time and only counting the ones that qualify — not multiplying by a ratio.
- [Recurring Date Schedules: Rules That Survive the Year](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/recurring-date-schedules/): A repeating schedule is a rule plus a set of exceptions, and the failure mode is baking the exceptions into the rule.
- [Documenting Employment Tenure and Anniversaries](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/documenting-employment-tenure/): Tenure records fail at handover, so the test of a good one is whether a stranger can rebuild the figure without asking you.
- [Planning Age Across Several Life Milestones at Once](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/age-on-multiple-milestones/): When one birth date has to be checked against a series of future dates, calculate each independently rather than stepping from one to the next.
- [A Date Input Checklist Worth Running Before You Calculate](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/calendar-date-quality-checklist/): Nearly every wrong date result comes from a wrong date input, and inputs are checkable in a way that outputs are not.
- [When a Calculator Is Not the Final Authority](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/calculator-results-official-decisions/): A calculator produces arithmetic. Whether that arithmetic decides anything depends on a rule it has no knowledge of.
- [What Actually Happens to the Dates You Type Into a Calculator](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/privacy-browser-calculators/): A browser-based calculator computes on your device, so the values never reach a server — but that is a property of how it is built, not a promise.
- [Korean Age Explained: Why Two Numbers Can Both Be Right](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/korean-age-explained/): Korean age counts calendar years rather than completed birthdays, so it can sit one or two years above international age for the same person.
- [East Asian Age Reckoning: Kazoedoshi, Virtual Age and Modern Practice](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/east-asian-age-reckoning/): Traditional year-count age appears across East Asia under different names, with different survival rates in modern official use.
- [Measuring Age in Quarters: When Three-Month Blocks Beat Years](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/age-in-quarters-guide/): Quarters give a coarser unit than months and a finer one than years, which suits reporting cycles, developmental checkpoints and cohort tracking.
- [ISO Week Numbering Explained: Week 1, Week-Years and the Dates They Cover](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/iso-week-numbering-explained/): ISO-8601 weeks always start on Monday and always contain a Thursday, which is why week 1 can begin in the previous December.
- [Fiscal Quarters Explained: Why Q1 Is Not Always January](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/fiscal-quarters-explained/): A fiscal quarter is a three-month block measured from an organisation's chosen financial year start, which is often not January.
- [Quarter End Dates: Planning Backwards From a Hard Deadline](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/quarter-end-dates-planning/): Quarter ends are fixed points that generate a cascade of earlier deadlines, and most of the risk sits in the days you did not count.
- [Calculating Working Hours Between Two Dates](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/working-hours-between-dates/): Working hours are a product of two decisions — which days count and how long a day is — and both need to be stated before the number means anything.
- [Time Zone Date Arithmetic: Why Two Clocks Disagree About Elapsed Time](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/timezone-date-arithmetic/): Local times are labels, not instants. Comparing them directly produces intervals that can be off by a full day.
- [Countdown Conventions: What 'Days Until' Actually Counts](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/countdown-conventions/): Two countdowns to the same date can differ by a day without either being wrong, because they disagree about whether today counts.
- [Holiday Countdown Maths: Fixed Dates, Moving Dates and Observed Dates](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/holiday-countdown-math/): Some holidays sit on the same date every year, some move with a lunar or ecclesiastical rule, and some shift when they land on a weekend.
- [Weeks Between Two Dates: Complete Weeks, Remainders and Part-Weeks](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/weeks-between-dates-guide/): A week count is a division with a remainder, and how you handle the remainder decides whether the answer is useful.
- [Day-Count Milestones: 1,000 Days, 10,000 Days and the Dates They Land On](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/day-count-milestones/): Day-count milestones are exact because they are pure addition — no month lengths, no leap-year adjustments, no convention to argue about.
- [Planning Milestone Birthdays at a Fixed Interval](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/milestone-birthday-intervals/): Milestone birthdays are calendar anniversaries, so they are found by adding whole years to a birth date rather than by adding days.
- [Quarter Birthdays and Other Fractional Birthday Traditions](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/quarter-birthday-explained/): A quarter birthday is three calendar months after a birth date, and like half birthdays it needs an end-of-month rule to be well defined.
- [Reverse Due Date Calculation: Working Backwards From Gestational Age](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/reverse-due-date-explained/): If you know the current gestational age, you can recover the implied last menstrual period and project the estimated due date from it.
- [IVF Due Dates: Why Transfer Date Gives a More Precise Estimate](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/ivf-due-date-dating/): With IVF the conception date is known rather than estimated, so the due date is calculated from the transfer date and the embryo's age.
- [Pregnancy Countdowns: Reading Days Remaining Alongside Gestational Age](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/pregnancy-countdown-guide/): A countdown to a due date and a gestational age describe the same pregnancy from opposite ends, and each is useful for different questions.
- [Working Days in a Month: Why the Count Swings by Three](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/working-days-in-month/): Months contain between 19 and 23 weekdays before holidays, which is enough variation to distort any monthly plan built on an average.
- [Calculating a Notice Period End Date](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/notice-period-calculation/): Notice periods can be defined in working days, calendar days, weeks or months, and each definition produces a different end date from the same start.
- [Probation Period End Dates and the Review That Should Precede Them](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/probation-period-end-dates/): A probation period defined in months ends on a calendar anniversary, and the review that decides its outcome has to happen before that date.
- [Long Service Milestones: Continuous Service and the Dates That Break It](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/long-service-leave-dates/): Long service entitlements depend on continuous service, which is a defined term rather than simply the time since the start date.
- [Term Date Planning: Building a Repeating Academic Schedule](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/term-date-planning/): A term schedule is a repeating rule plus a set of exceptions, and the exceptions are what make it worth calculating rather than typing.
- [Measuring Semester Length in Weeks, Days and Teaching Time](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/semester-length-planning/): A semester has a calendar length and a teaching length, and the gap between them is where planning goes wrong.
- [Calculating Age at Marriage for Records and Genealogy](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/age-at-marriage-records/): Age on a wedding date is a straightforward calendar calculation, but the records it comes from often are not.
- [Sleep Debt Arithmetic: What the Number Can and Cannot Tell You](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/sleep-debt-arithmetic/): Sleep debt is a simple subtraction repeated across nights, and its usefulness depends entirely on the target you subtract from.
- [Lifetime Screen Time Estimates and Why They Are So Sensitive](https://www.agecalculatorlab.com/articles/screen-time-estimates/): Lifetime totals multiply a daily average across thousands of days, which magnifies any error in the average by the same factor.
